topic: How solar and lunar eclipses work
title: How does the Moon cover the Sun? 🌑☀️
hook: How can the tiny Moon completely cover the enormous Sun?

scenes.narration: How can the tiny Moon completely cover the enormous Sun?
scenes.on_screen_text: How does the Moon cover the Sun?

scenes.narration: The Sun is about four hundred times wider than the Moon, but it's also about four hundred times farther away.
So from Earth, both look almost the same size in the sky.
In a solar eclipse, the Moon lines up right in front and its shadow falls on the Earth.
But that shadow is small: only people inside a narrow strip see the total eclipse.
So why isn't there one every month? Because the Moon's orbit is tilted about five degrees, so it usually passes above or below.
In a lunar eclipse it's the other way around: the Earth blocks the Sun and the Moon slips into our shadow.
And it turns red, because Earth's atmosphere bends the light of every sunrise and sunset on the planet onto it.
And since the Moon drifts away almost four centimeters a year, in hundreds of millions of years there will be no more total eclipses.
Send this to someone you'd watch the next eclipse with.

description: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, so they look the same size. In a solar eclipse the Moon's shadow falls on a narrow strip of Earth; it doesn't happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted about 5°. In a lunar eclipse the Moon turns red from light that Earth's atmosphere bends toward it. The Moon drifts away about 3.8 cm a year. Original 3D animation; not to scale.

claims.statement: The Sun's diameter is about 400 times the Moon's, and it is also about 400 times farther away.
The Moon's orbit is inclined about 5° to the ecliptic, so eclipses don't happen every month.
An eclipsed Moon looks reddish because of light refracted by Earth's atmosphere.
The Moon recedes about 3.8 cm per year; in hundreds of millions of years total solar eclipses will no longer occur.
